result:
The town had a library for things people had forgotten.

Not lost things. Lost things were handled by a woman at the railway station, who kept umbrellas in a barrel and had strong opinions about gloves.

Forgotten things required more careful storage.

There were drawers of childhood passwords, shelves of half-finished songs, and a climate-controlled room containing the exact blue of a kitchen that had been painted over in 1987.

You could borrow your own memories for two weeks. Renewals were permitted unless someone else remembered them too.

One afternoon, a man came in asking for the sound of his father laughing.

“Any particular occasion?” the librarian asked.

“No,” he said. Then, after a moment: “I used to know.”

She checked the catalogue.

They tried a birthday, a fishing trip, and an incident involving a ladder. None was right. The man apologized each time, as though he were being difficult about a perfectly good meal.

At last she brought out a small, unlabelled box.

Inside was an ordinary Tuesday. His father stood at the kitchen sink, sleeves rolled up, laughing at something the man himself had said. Neither of them had thought to remember what it was.

“Yes,” the man said.

The librarian left him alone with it.

When he returned to the desk, he asked what would happen if he forgot to bring it back.

“We’ll send a reminder.”

“And if I forget that?”

She slid a library card across the counter.

“Is this still your address?”

He looked at it. His childhood home.

“No,” he said, and borrowed her pen.
